title: Pleasing God · Chapter 1: Pleasing God
speaker: Joshua Heward-Mills
text:
Chapter 1

# Pleasing God

Therefore, whether we are at home [on earth] or away from home [and with Him], it is our [constant] ambition to be pleasing to Him. For we [believers will be called to account and] must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may be repaid for what has been done in the body, whether good or bad [that is, each will be held responsible for his actions, purposes, goals, motives—the use or misuse of his time, opportunities and abilities].

2 Corinthians 5:9-10 (AMP)

The determiner of life, the determiner of your life, is God.

During a teaching session, I asked a doctor about completing housemanship. The doctor explained that the consultant responsible for a particular department had to sign the doctor out. I asked whether the approval of the nurses, the receptionist, or even the patients could take the place of that signature. It could not. A patient might feel that the doctor had provided excellent care, but the consultant still had to approve the work. Even a consultant from another department could not simply take the place of the one responsible.

That doctor gave us insight into the spirit world. To become a doctor, there's a person who has to be happy with you. In the spirit world, the Scripture tells us that promotion—any form of upward mobility, climbing, or increase—doesn't come from the east, the west, or the south. God is the decider. He's the consultant. He's the One who signs off.

For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.

Psalm 75:6-7 (KJV)

God is the judge. He sets one up; He puts one down. Hey, if you are down, don't blame your husband. It's not because of your wife. It's not because of your lecturer. If your bank account is down, don't blame the government. Put the axe at the root. God has not signed off. He has not endorsed what you are doing. What's going on in your heart determines a lot about how your life will go—not what's going on in your head or with your hands. What's going on in your heart?

I have known what I'm saying since I was about twenty or twenty-one years old. I knew that nobody could control my life. Nobody could put me down. Trust me, people have tried. Even I can't put myself down or up. But the consultant—I've always been aware of Him.

# 1. Becoming a Christian should change your aim.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)

If any man is in Christ, he's a new creature. So my question is: what becomes new? It's not your clothes. It's not your height. It's not your hair. It's not your face. It's not even your temperament. What are the things that are supposed to change? I think the biggest change is your goal in life—your aims.

What are you living for? What do you want your life to accomplish? Everybody has an aim, whether or not that aim has been carefully considered. Becoming a believer should affect the purpose behind everything you do.

Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed? (For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.

Matthew 6:31-32 (KJV)

The Passion Translation puts it this way:

“So then, forsake your worries! Why would you say, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’ For that is what the unbelievers chase after. Doesn’t your heavenly Father already know the things your bodies require?

Matthew 6:31-32 (TPT)

Jesus described the things the Gentiles seek: what they will eat, what they will drink, and what they will wear. These things can become the whole pursuit of a person's life. But a Christian is meant to have a different governing aim.

In the New International Version, Paul says:

So we make it our goal to please him, whether we are at home in the body or away from it.

2 Corinthians 5:9 (NIV)

We make it our goal to please Him. Whether we are at home in the body or away from it—alive or dead. The Amplified Bible calls it our constant ambition. Pleasing Him is to be our constant ambition. Alive or dead, on earth or with Him, this is the aim.

When you become a believer, your life's aim should change. That's what becomes new about you: you have a different aim from the person you are sitting next to at work. I find that missing in the church today. We don't have an aim to please God. It's almost like we are allowed to be saved and have other aims. But it's not true. It's a false theology. We make it our aim to please Him.

The next verse explains why: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. We will account for what we have done. Our actions, purposes, and motives matter to Him. Our lives are not merely a performance for the people around us.

# 2. Examine the ambitions you have accepted.

What's the vision you have for your life? It shouldn't be to live in America. I want you to know, as a pastor, it's a very evil aim for somebody to have. Neither should it be to have a big church. Hold on—it is not a good aim to have. These are the aims Christians have. Christians even have an aim to be happy. I don't know where you learned that from.

I have one aim, one singular purpose and vision, one thing that wakes me up every morning: to be pleasing to Him. It is my constant ambition. It's my aim.

There is a difference between wanting a large church for your own importance and wanting to fulfil the vision the Holy Spirit has given you. If God gives a person a vision for twenty-five thousand saved souls, the person can pursue that vision in order to please Him. The size of the church is then subject to obedience. It is not an independent ambition competing with God.

I have no aim to live in Ghana. I have no aim to be the pastor of the First Love Centre. I don't have any of these hidden motives, by the grace of God, by the mercies of God. I pray it is so. I have an aim to be pleasing to God. That's my goal. If that means being a pastor of six people, so be it. A pastor of a million people, so be it.

This is what leads to disappointment and sadness amongst Christians: you had an aim to be happily married. So when it doesn't happen, you become disappointed. But the one who has an aim to please God is never disappointed. Your biggest life's aim is to finish your PhD, to get married, to have a child. “I need to have a child.” That's all you ever think about. That's all you slave over. That's what leads to sadness.

But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.

1 Timothy 6:9 (KJV)

People who want to get rich are tempted. You see, a lot of temptations would not be there if you didn't want to be rich. When you possess a goal to be rich, you've given Satan a window for temptation.

When I was about fourteen, I was in a shop with my parents. An older man approached me in the bathroom and offered me a large amount of money for a sexual act. I called for my mother. She came and confronted him. I had no desire for the money he was offering, so the money did not persuade me.

On another occasion, somebody whom the church had helped came to my office with a large amount of money. The person wanted to give it privately to me as a personal expression of thanks. I declined. The person spent a long time trying to convince me to accept it, but I did not need to be persuaded by it. I did not have the goal of becoming rich through such an arrangement.

When a person has decided, “I must have this standard of life,” the enemy has something with which to tempt that person. A Christian may sincerely want to be in church and still be repeatedly drawn away by a desire that has become a controlling goal.

Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man: But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.

James 1:13-15 (KJV)

Do not say that God is tempting you. Examine the desire within you. What is pulling you? What have you told yourself you must have? That desire may be giving temptation its opportunity.

Some of you have a goal to be right. “I just want to be right.” And you fight and fight and fight. Some of you, it's not even money. You want to be impressive to people. That's all. You don't say it like that because it sounds some way, but, “I want my friends to feel I made it. My Instagram must shine.”

Think of Adam before the fall. The question was what God had said to do. But Eve saw something that appeared desirable to her, and another desire came into the picture. When making ourselves happy becomes the deciding rule, the direction of our lives changes.

I recognise that this is a demanding message. It reaches deeper than the usual questions about what we would like to have. When I was considering marriage, my concern was to discover what would please God. Where a person worked, where the person came from, or other people's opinions could not become my highest test. I wanted to know what would make Him happy.

The same applies to ministry. When somebody asks whom we will invite to a conference, my concern cannot simply be a list of well-known names or the people who have asked to come. I want to find out what will please Him. If He wants a particular person to preach, that is the person I want.

Whether I'm asleep or have gone to heaven to be with Jesus, or I'm here on earth—whether I'm breathing, working, preaching—I have one singular aim: not to please you or any other human being on this earth. I just want to be pleasing to God. When that switch turns in your heart, you've probably had the greatest seismic shift in the course of your life. You start saying, “God, are You happy with me?”

# 3. Pleasure and importance cannot satisfy your soul.

I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity. I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it? I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life. I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees: I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts. So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me. And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.

Ecclesiastes 2:1-11 (KJV)

Here is a man who tried pleasure. He tried laughter, wine, great projects, houses, vineyards, gardens, wealth, music, and the things his eyes desired. He became important. He had the opportunity to experience what many people spend their lives pursuing. Then he looked at it all and described it as vanity and a chasing after the wind.

What is your life's aim? To become rich? To marry? To pass an examination? To move abroad? To own a new car? Many people have never carefully examined the purpose to which they have given their lives.

Allow me, on behalf of the Holy Spirit, to introduce you to another option: to live and to please God.

People live for the approval of men. You want me to say you are doing well, and if I don't say you're doing well, you are finished. That is idol worship, and you'll never be satisfied. Paul said, “Heaven or earth, dead or alive, today or tomorrow, I live for one thing: to be pleasing.”

Jesus (to the Pharisees) : You’ve made your choice. Your ambition is to look good in front of other people, not God. But God sees through to your hearts. He values things differently from you. The goals you and your peers are reaching for God detests.

Luke 16:15 (VOICE)

God values differently from man. A thing can be highly esteemed among people and still be an abomination before Him. That should make us examine our ambitions. Are we trying to look good before people, or are we trying to be pleasing to God?

The desire to be loved or liked can also control a person. Somebody longs to be held, admired, or made to feel special, and that desire keeps leading the person into relationships and decisions that do not please God.

Another person wants importance. Jesus spoke about people who did their works to be seen by men and loved places of honour. I try to be careful about things that make me appear great, because I do not want my ambition to shift from pleasing God to becoming important.

But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments, And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi.

Matthew 23:5-7 (KJV)

I have experienced joy in the midst of great sadness. It is possible to be crying and yet to have a soul that is satisfied in God. Pleasure and the absence of pain are not the same thing as that satisfaction.

Whatever aim has taken the place of pleasing God, allow the Holy Spirit to work on your heart. Go to work to please Him. Earn your salary to please Him. Preach to please Him. Let the purpose reach into everything you do.

# 4. Pleasing God changes the questions you ask at home.

Having an aim to be impressive to other people causes a fake life. If I have an aim that my marriage should impress you, that's different from having a good marriage. They're two different things. I can post a picture and say, “Eight years and counting. It's been a blessed journey with you, babe.” Then everybody says, “Wow!” But if I have a vision to please God, I'll be assessing myself as a husband and asking, “Are my prayers even hindered?”

As a husband, am I doing what His Word requires? Are my prayers hindered? Am I providing for my household? Have I become bitter against my wife?

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.

1 Peter 3:7 (KJV)

But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

1 Timothy 5:8 (KJV)

Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.

Colossians 3:19 (KJV)

Everybody may be clapping for me while God sees something He does not approve. Human congratulations do not answer the questions His Word asks.

The same applies to a wife. People can admire her appearance and think highly of her, but what does God value?

Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

1 Peter 3:3-4 (KJV)

Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her. Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.

Proverbs 31:28-31 (KJV)

If pleasing God is the aim, the question is no longer merely, “What are other people saying about me?” It becomes, “What is the testimony of the person who lives with me? Is my spirit pleasing to God?”

Some people have an aim not to be cheated. “It will be fair and square. Since you won't submit, I won't provide. Since you won't provide, I won't submit.” So we'll be playing table tennis at home, because my aim is fair and square. My aim is not to please God. But if my aim is to please God, I want to be the best of husbands. I want to be the best of wives before Him—not before anybody else, before God.

If I sat at home reading every birthday and Christmas card I have received, I could conclude that I am the best pastor in the world. But God sees differently. I need more than people's appreciation to know how I stand before Him.

# 5. Choose His approval when your pride is being tested.

Even writing a song presents a question of aim. Do you want it to become popular, or do you want God to be pleased with it? Those are different concerns, and they can guide the work in different directions.

I knew of a situation in which a pastor was asked to step aside so that an assistant could take over. Another minister found it impossible to accept sitting under the person who had previously been assisting. But what was the aim—to preach, to avoid embarrassment, or to please God?

When the aim changes, a test can become an opportunity to please Him. We can recognise that humility matters to Him and allow Him to work in us instead of fighting merely to protect our position.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

Psalm 51:17 (KJV)

But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.

Job 23:10 (KJV)

If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.

Job 14:14 (KJV)

People scramble for things that cannot be compared with the honour of being pleasing to God. Even having this as your aim is precious. I am not saying that you will never fall short. I am saying that this should be the goal of your heart.

Somebody once told me that I had a great deal of self-control. I explained that what I was conscious of was God. I am aware that He is watching, and I do not want my response to displease Him.

Think of a child appointed to write down the names of those talking in class. Somebody whose name has been written down challenges the child, and the child answers back. Now the child has also spoken and must put another name on the list. I do not want to respond to somebody's wrong in a way that makes me guilty too.

I have been despised, insulted, disregarded, and confronted in ministry. Yet I do not want another person's conduct to determine my response. I want to consider what God will say about my own words and actions.

There have been times when I have said something to my wife and then gone out to the car. As I reached for the door, I became concerned about whether God was happy with what I had said. I went back and apologised. Sometimes she was surprised. My concern was not simply whether she would remain angry until evening. I was thinking about Him.

When I search the Scriptures, I am trying to find out what He is not happy with. His Word must have the freedom to correct me.

On a visit to a minister, I took a gift but initially forgot to hand it over because our conversation had occupied my mind. After leaving, I remembered and returned. I met the assistant helping with the meeting and asked that the gift be passed on. The assistant suggested that I should give it personally so that the minister would know and appreciate it. But that was not why I had come. I was not trying to obtain personal recognition or a connection. I wanted to do what was right before God.

We are human and weak. Our aims can drift. We can begin serving God and find ourselves pursuing something else. That is why we must keep returning to the question of whom we are trying to please.

Serving God is not simply saying, “I want to preach.” It is saying, “Anything, anytime, anywhere.” If He needs me to sweep, I will sweep. If circumstances require me to take a job, I must still be willing to serve. My salary or position cannot be the thing that makes me His servant.

# 6. Live in the sight of God.

Do not assume that God is happy with something merely because it looks spiritual. As pastors, this is one of our great temptations. A seemingly spiritual vision can conceal a personal ambition.

David had it in his heart to build a house for the Lord, but God told him that he would not be the one to build it.

And David said to Solomon, My son, as for me, it was in my mind to build an house unto the name of the LORD my God: But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build an house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight.

1 Chronicles 22:7-8 (KJV)

Something can appear admirable to us while God wants something different from us. We must find out what He is asking, rather than assuming that every impressive religious project must have His approval.

Live for an audience of One. Play your instrument for Him. Assess your life before Him. There is a theological expression, coram Deo: to live in the sight of God. Be conscious that He is watching now.

Do not make greatness, wealth, a particular place to live, marriage, a child, importance, or the approval of a particular human being your governing aim. Have one central purpose: spend your life seeking to make God happy with you.

# 7. Let even your giving be pleasing to Him.

When Paul received the gift brought by Epaphroditus, he described it as well pleasing to God. Paul was the one receiving the gift, but God's pleasure was what mattered.

But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.

Philippians 4:18 (KJV)

The same aim must govern our giving. It is not enough to impress the person who receives something. Let the gift and the heart behind it be acceptable to God.

Think also of Enoch's testimony.

By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

Hebrews 11:5 (KJV)

Hebrews 11 tells of men and women whose faith produced remarkable things. Enoch's testimony is that he pleased God. What a testimony to have!

Paul also describes the aim of his instruction.

Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:

1 Timothy 1:5 (KJV)

Instruction should have an aim. My aim in sharing this teaching is that your life will change at its centre. You should be able to look back and recognise that a new purpose took hold of you: I want to please God.
